“Come Byron, come to me.”

Her voice was soft and mellow, and each word had a lilt to it like a song. She beckoned to him with her outstretched hands.

She was more beautiful than anything he had ever seen. Her hair cascaded down around her shoulders like rivers of the night sky. She moved her slender frame more gracefully than even the citadel’s most talented dancers.

“It is ok Byron, come to me.”

She smiled as she began to move forward, her body moving with the gentle stride of a cat’s. Her hand remained outstretched, calling him to accept it.

But he couldn’t. He had a wife. He loved his wife. And his family, he could not leave them. The boys would be fine, but how would Cecile care for the girls? They were so young still, his little angels…how would he himself live without them?

“They will understand, do not worry about them. You know what you want.”

How did she know? Perhaps his face betrayed him. She was close now. He could see the starlight reflect off of her ice-blue eyes. Her bare feet padded softly on the damp grass, the end of her midnight black dress dancing near her ankles. She raised her hand and placed it on his shoulder, caressing his arm and staring at him with those eyes. He could smell the fragrance of spring on her, a mix of flowers and the indescribable vitality of life.

No. He must fight. He had a family to protect. They would be helpless without him. He hadn’t fought through the war to leave them now. He took a step back, just outside of the woman’s reach.

“Now Byron, you know you cannot resist, no man has ever resisted my call. You’ve been through a lot in this war. You are in need of relief, an escape. I can provide that. You will never have to endure that pain again.”

The war... The memories were still fresh in his mind. The blood, the screaming. He saw children slain in the streets. He saw his shield brothers slaughtered. And the torture, the torture was worst of all. Countless days spent screaming in agony, yet refusing to yield. They had mutilated and traumatized him. The smell of burning flesh would overwhelm him and he would black out from the pain. Then the day came when he was freed. He remembered the horrified look on the soldiers who came to save them as they gazed upon his face. He didn't remember much of what happened after that. He didn't really want to. What would his wife think? Would she still love him? His own children would be terrified of him…

“Byron, stop this worrying, I am here. That is all that matters, embrace what is inevitable.”

Suddenly she was there again, tracing her finger across his chest. She drew him into her embrace. Her lips were like the softest velvet and her hair fell like curtains around him, sealing both of them off from the world, the world full of pain and suffering. Her presence overcame him and nothing else mattered. He melted into her arms while the world and all of his pain dissolved around him.

“We tried to fetch you as soon as we could, my lady”

The old man bowed his head and backed up, giving her room to gaze upon her husband’s face, or what was left of it. Her hands trembled, but she forced back the tears. She had to be strong. She could not show weakness, not to him now. His eyes were closed, as if he were blocking out the world. Nothing had ever cut her as deep as when she had heard the news, brought to her by a common messenger boy. Frankly, she was surprised to see him return at all. Her voice came out in tremors.

“I…I won’t accept it. No, not my love, my kind, gentle love. The one who protected us, cared for us, and provided for us. Why now? After all of this, when we could finally be a family again.”

She realized her face was wet. She could not hold it back, tears streamed down her face. He continued to close his eyes as if nothing had happened.

The old man cleared his throat. His eyes were sorrowful. He knew the pain she was feeling. He had known love and loss.

“If I may, my lady, the pain he suffered was more than any man I have ever known. The Lady Thana offered him a relief and escape from the agony. It is true what they say, she is irresistible, and all men heed her call. She is indeed a harsh mistress.”

Cecile fell to her knees and sobbed as the man placed the white cloth over her husband’s face.

He retired early and thought he’d build a pond, deep enough to stand in and long enough to swim laps. He was still in good shape, had two acres, why not? He always liked ponds; the wildlife, the cattails, the crickets at night. What else was he going to do - golf? Remarry?

He didn’t know much about how to build a pond, but wasn’t a pond just a hole with water in it? He could do that. He’d dug holes before.

He started a few days after he first thought of it, digging a few hours here, a few hours there, until it began to consume him. He couldn’t think of anything but the pond and what he was going to do with it. He was going to swim in it, have a picnic when his kids visited. He’d put a sign out front advertising it, though it’d be free.

Three weeks in he had already dug a few feet deep by a few feet wide. It was starting to look like something. A koi pond, he thought.

He bought a bench at an estate sale and placed it at the mouth of the pond. This is where the visitors would sit while he told them about how he built it himself. This is what he thought about on his breaks.

At two months in it was getting deep enough at some points that he would soon need to install ropes and pulleys to hoist himself, and the dirt, out. That he could do.

At three months a story was written about him after the boy at the hardware store who asked him why he was buying what he was buying told his friend who worked part-time at the newspaper. He was proud, and it brought unexpected attention. Fathers brought their children to help and used it as a teachable moment.

See, if you put your mind to something, you can do anything.

Many hands make light work.

The help didn’t last long, but he didn’t mind. He was getting closer to finishing it, at least the digging. He had given some thought as to how he’d finish it, but figured he would fill it up with water from his hose. He liked the idea of just spraying water into it, sitting on the bench with the hose in the air like a geyser.

That it was May helped him save on time and water, the downpours filling up his pond as lightning spread across the prairie.

In June he had to get started earlier; by mid-day the heat was too much. He’d spend the rest of the day inside. Then at twilight he’d get back out for the last hour of sunlight.

By August he’d finished, just in time for the pond to be most useful. From a telephone pole at the end of his driveway he hung a sign: “PRAIRIE LIGHT POND: OPEN TO ALL. GOOD FOR SWIMMING. FREE OF CHARGE.”

For the rest of August and into September he found the occasional stranger or young family at his door, eager to host and make their brief experience a pleasant one. He’d make lemonade and tell them his story of how he built the pond. They’d listen in disbelief or confusion, unsure of what to make of him. But they had a good time.

In October he died in his sleep, found by one of his neighbors who hadn’t seen him at the pond in a few days. His children sold the house to an elderly woman who built a few additions onto the house. The following summer she drained the pond, installed a fence, built a pool, and took down the sign facing the road at the end of the driveway.
